question.text: A 45-year-old man presents for his annual checkup. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes mellitus (DM) type 2 that is well-controlled with diet. In addition, he was admitted to this hospital 1-year ago for a myocardial infarction (MI). The patient reports a 40-pack-year smoking history. However, after his MI, his doctors informed him about how detrimental smoking was to his heart condition. Since then, he has made efforts to cut down and now, for the last six months, has stopped smoking. He says he used to use smoking as a means of dealing with his work and family stresses. He now attends wellness sessions at work and meditates early every morning before the family wakes up. Which of the following stages of the transtheoretical model is this patient most likely in?

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has stopped smoking for six months, which is a significant and sustained change. He is also attending wellness sessions and meditating, indicating a commitment to improving his health. These behaviors suggest he is in the maintenance stage of change.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The patient has stopped smoking for six months and is actively engaging in wellness activities.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Precontemplation: The patient is not in precontemplation because he has already stopped smoking. Contemplation: While he may be considering quitting, the six-month duration of abstinence suggests he is beyond the contemplation stage. Preparation: The patient has already taken action (quitting smoking) and is maintaining that behavior. Action: The patient has already taken action (quitting smoking) and is maintaining that behavior. Therefore, maintenance is the most accurate stage.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has stopped smoking for six months and is actively engaging in stress-reduction activities like meditation and wellness sessions, indicating a clear action phase. While he acknowledges the harm of smoking, his sustained abstinence and new coping strategies place him in the Preparation stage, which precedes Action. However, since he has already taken concrete steps (stopped smoking and changed behaviors), the best fit is Preparation, as it reflects the period before taking action but after contemplation.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The patient has stopped smoking for six months and now engages in stress-reduction activities, indicating a shift toward action.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: None directly applicable; the question focuses on stages of change, not medical diagnosis.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has successfully quit smoking for six months, which is a sustained behavior change. He is now engaging in healthy coping mechanisms (wellness sessions, meditation) and has no current relapse. This aligns with the Maintenance stage, where individuals work to prevent relapse and sustain their new behavior over time. His past smoking history and recent cessation indicate he has moved beyond the initial stages of change.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: The patient has stopped smoking for the last six months and is actively maintaining his quit status with healthy behavioral substitutions.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Precontemplation (no intention to change), Contemplation (thinking about quitting), Preparation (planning to quit soon), and Action (within the last 6 months of quitting) were considered but ruled out because the patient has already surpassed the 6-month mark and is actively maintaining his behavior, not preparing or contemplating.

openbio_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is most likely in the Preparation stage of the transtheoretical model. This is indicated by his recent efforts to cut down on smoking and his cessation of smoking for the last six months. He has also adopted healthy coping mechanisms such as attending wellness sessions at work and meditating in the morning. olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has quit smoking for six months after a prior MI and is now managing his diabetes well with diet, indicating a sustained behavior change. The transtheoretical model progression—awareness, contemplation, action, maintenance—aligns with this description, where sustained abstinence after an initial action phase typically places the individual in maintenance.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: The patient reports stopping smoking for six months and has made efforts to manage stress through alternative methods (meditation, wellness sessions), suggesting he has maintained the behavior change post-cessation.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Preparation (trying to quit but not yet successful), Action (actively trying to quit within the last 6 months), and others are less likely because he has already been smoke-free for six months, which is characteristic of the maintenance stage.
